svg.text: LIQUID-SEALED PRESSURE BELL, REV F, Ø150, M3 ROD, PLA PAN — reference source for SDP810 qualification
The load HANGS BELOW, submerged, so it stabilises the bell instead of capsizing it. No guide, no bearings, no friction. PLA + stainless washers. All dimensions mm.
SUPERSEDES REV A (free-floating, capsizes), REV B (guide rod, adds friction), REV C (Ø180, 1350 g), REV D (Ø6 Al rod) and REV E (nut + backing washer). Do not build any of them.

g.text: drawn at 500 Pa, the worst case for submersion. ONLY THE BELL AND THE HANGING LOAD ARE CRITICAL.
M3 stainless rod, SCREWED into a tapped hub
Ø80 stainless washers — the load AND the ballast
PLA pan Ø90 × 2.5, on an M3 nut
no core — the middle is free for the load to hang in
The stack top must stay below the INNER surface at every point. 500 Pa is the worst case, because h is largest there, and it is what is
drawn: 101 mm from the lid to the inner surface against 126 mm to the stack top. Hold d near 65 with the supply and read it off the skirt.
The outer level rises ~28 mm from tare to 500 Pa, so size the tub depth for the HIGH state and the pan-to-floor clearance for the LOW one.

svg.text: 1 — SKIRT
unchanged from rev A. Print RIM DOWN.
wall 0.80 — 2 perimeters at a 0.4 nozzle, no top/bottom, no infill
graduations every 5, numbered every 25, ZERO AT THE RIM, 0.4 proud
first layer is the sealing edge, so it comes off the plate flat and square
use a brim — a thin 150 dia. ring lifts at a corner and goes oval
2 — LID
print TOP FACE DOWN. Collar, ribs and hub grow upward.
underside, looking up
section
disc Ø150.0 × 0.8; collar Ø148.4 OD × 12 × 1.2, skirt slips OVER it
6 ribs 1.2 wide × 10 tall, r12 → r73, same side as the collar
CENTRAL HUB Ø16 × 25, TAPPED M3 RIGHT THROUGH the lid. Print the thread or
tap it — 25 mm of M3 in PLA shears at ~3.5 kN against the 9 N it carries.
A tapped hub makes the rod REMOVABLE, so the rod-less point is an M3×6 grub
screw, not electrical tape: repeatable, and its mass is known. Squareness is
uncritical — an off-axis hang changes nothing in the formula.
Glue the skirt joint with CA. A pinhole leak costs supply flow, not accuracy.
3 — ROD, PAN AND WASHERS
M3 STAINLESS threaded rod, 185 long. Lighter than
the Ø6 aluminium it replaces (8.2 g against 14.1 g),
because area beats density: 5.6 mm² against 28.3.
and it drops the Al/stainless galvanic pair, which
would have changed the mass over a season.
PAN: PLA Ø90 × 2.5 on an M3 nut,
150 below the lid. PRINT IT SOLID — see note 7.
WASHERS: Ø80 stainless, 923 g dry for 500 Pa,
166 g for 125 Pa, 24 mm of stack at full load. An
optional PLA sleeve Ø3.2/Ø12.8 centres their bores.
4 — TUB AND STANDPIPE
uncritical — neither appears in the formula
≥200 ID at the bell’s working depth, ≥180 inside depth, ~4 L of water.
A tapered bucket is fine: the taper changes how far the levels move,
not the pressure, because d is read rather than assumed.
STANDPIPE Ø6 rigid tube, siliconed through the tub floor at r = 57 — midway
between the Ø80 washers and the skirt, 17 clear of each, 148 above the floor.
its mouth must be ABOVE the inner water surface at every pressure, and
BELOW the lid at every pressure. Check both after you fill it.
It replaces the rev A/B core, whose only remaining job this was. Deleting
the core is what freed the middle for the hanging load.
CONSTANTS AND WORKING FORMULA
P = km · mapp − kd · d
mapp = (bell + lid + rod, DRY) + 0.8736 × (stainless, DRY) + 0.195 × (PLA pan, DRY)
The rod is NOT in the buoyancy term — its submerged length varies with d, so it lives in kd via Arod . Only the ALWAYS submerged
pieces take a ratio: the washers and nut at 0.8736, the PLA pan at 0.195. calibrationBellWeighing.svg shows the rig.
MEASURE THE RATIO, DO NOT TABLE IT. 1 % of assumed density = 0.145 % of P, and washer grades run 7.70 (430) to 8.00 (316) —
0.56 % of reading, 2.8 Pa at 500 against a 1.3 Pa budget. Weigh the batch hydrostatically (0.013 %) or by displacement (0.12 %).
A magnet separates 430/410 from 304/316 and halves the range, but cold-worked 304 is weakly magnetic, so it indicates rather than decides.
km = g / Aeff
Aeff = π·ID²/4 − rod bore
kd = ρg(Awall + Arod ) / Aeff
skirt AND rod pierce the surface now
nominal ID 148.4, rod M3
Aeff = 17 289 mm²
Awall = 375; rod 7.07 at the lid, 5.62 at the surface
MEASURE THE FINISHED PART. Two perpendicular IDs at the rim: Aeff = πd₁d₂/4 − πdrod ²/4.
RANGE 42.8 Pa → 500 Pa · 1 g = 0.567 Pa · 500 Pa = 923 g dry · 125 Pa = 166 g dry
SECOND CONFIGURATION, ROD AND PAN OFF, M3×6 GRUB SCREW FITTED: km = 0.5670 Pa/g, kd = 0.2122 Pa/mm, floor 36.3 Pa
Its value is a MODEL CHECK, not a ladder point — it only reaches 5.2 Pa lower, but it moves BOTH constants, so agreeing with the rodded fit validates the whole model.
YOUR SCALE IS THE REFERENCE, AND ITS SPAN MATTERS FAR MORE THAN ITS RESOLUTION.
P scales directly with the scale’s gain, so an unchecked span goes straight through. At 500 Pa: 0.57 % on a 1 g scale with the span
unchecked, 0.26 % with it checked to ±0.1 %, 0.20 % on a 0.1 g scale — by which point the AREA term dominates. Buy one calibration weight,
not a better scale, and check it near the working mass. Even the unchecked column is 5× better than the part’s 3 % span spec.
Weigh the whole assembly before and after every session: a change is water ingress into the bell, and it invalidates the session.
WHY THIS ONE STANDS UP, AND WHAT TO WATCH
STABILITY NOW RISES WITH LOAD. The stabilising mass and the applied mass are the same object. Tilt stiffness: +0.04 N·m/rad
bare, +0.27 at 125 Pa, +1.24 at 500 Pa — against rev A’s −0.14 at 500 Pa, which is what capsized it on the bench.
DO NOT HANG A FIXED BALLAST INSTEAD. Stabilising weight below the lid and the pressure floor are the SAME quantity. ~333 g of
apparent ballast at 150 mm would buy the full-load stiffness and put ~190 Pa on the floor. Only the applied load can pay for its own stability.
And running ROD-LESS with weights on the lid is rev A again. Bare is safe; 72 g (77 Pa) keeps two thirds of the bare margin; it capsizes at
276 g, i.e. 192 Pa. The bench has already shown that this margin cannot be felt until it goes, so treat the bare point as the only rod-less one.
THE STACK MUST STAY BELOW THE INNER WATER SURFACE at every point, and 500 Pa is the worst case because h is largest there.
Ø80 washers keep 117 cm³ to 24 mm of stack, putting the top 126 mm below the lid against 101 mm to the inner surface. Ø50 would be 64 mm and would emerge.
Bubbles on smooth stainless are a 0.1–0.3 Pa effect, not a 0.4 Pa one — a 1 cm³ bubble is 12 mm across and you would see it. Wet and tap
the stack before lowering it, load any dished washer concave-DOWN, and let the repeat readings §2.5 already requires catch the rest.
PRINT THE PAN SOLID. A 1 cm³ internal void is 1 g of buoyancy = 0.57 Pa, and a void that slowly floods moves the tare with nothing
to show it. PLA density itself barely matters — the pan is nearly neutrally buoyant, so a 1 % density error is 0.09 Pa. Voids matter six times more.
KEEP THE SENSOR AT THE HEIGHT OF THE BELL’S WATER LINE, or correct at 0.0118 Pa/mm of air column. 100 mm is 1.2 Pa, which is 1 %
of a 125 Pa point. This applies to every version of this rig and was missing from revs A and B.
Changing washers means lifting the bell out and re-settling. That is the price of having no bearings, and it is the only thing rev B did better.
